Chapter 7: The Ongoing Struggle for Accountability
As the dust began to settle, one question just wouldn’t go away—who was really going to be held accountable? Uncovering the truth was just the start. Making sure there were real consequences, well, that was a whole different story.
Institutions, now under the spotlight, scrambled to respond. Some kicked off internal investigations. Others put out statements, promising change. But you and I both know—promises are easy to make, and a whole lot harder to keep.
Picture this: one HR manager, stuck right in the middle. She’s torn between loyalty to her company and her own sense of justice. She wants to believe things will be different this time, that maybe—just maybe—the old habit of sweeping problems under the rug is finally over.
But as the weeks go by, she starts to see the same old patterns creeping back in. Whispered warnings. Quiet transfers. And this stubborn reluctance to confront those at the very top. Most people don’t realize just how deeply rooted these habits are—or how much pushback there is against real, meaningful change.
Meanwhile, the journalists kept watching. They noticed that some organizations really tried—putting new policies in place, rolling out training programs, and sometimes even holding people accountable for abusing their power.
But they also saw where the system broke down. There were always doubters—people who questioned the stories, wondered about the motives of those who came forward, or worried more about reputational damage than about actual justice.
Now, for the survivors, this fight for accountability could be absolutely exhausting. Some ended up reliving old traumas as investigations dragged on. Others faced backlash from colleagues and friends who felt betrayed when they spoke out. It became clear: accountability isn’t just about punishing the guilty. It’s about changing a whole culture—the one that let abuse thrive in the first place.
The journalists saw that their work was far from done. They kept following up on leads, checking in with sources, and holding institutions to their word. They knew change wouldn’t happen overnight, and that there would be setbacks. But they also started to see something new—a real willingness to listen, and a growing understanding that staying silent just wasn’t an option anymore.
